Footsteps, vendors’ voices, rustling bags and the occasional squeak of a handcart overlap; fabric awnings flutter slightly when air moves through. People dress in everyday shirts, trousers or abayas. A seller may welcome someone with تفضل, while customers open with السلام عليكم and address the seller as أخوي or أستاذ.

Basra Times Square mall is a modern shopping setting: a large, clean-lined exterior with glass entrances, bright commercial signs and cars approaching paved parking areas. Inside, polished floors reflect ceiling lights and illuminated shopfronts; escalators carry people smoothly between levels while families walk at a slower pace. Store signs can mix Arabic and English. Automatic doors slide with a soft motor sound, under music, footsteps and conversation. The contrast with Basra’s hot, hazy daylight is noticeable at the entrance. Visitors wear everyday Iraqi clothes, from T-shirts and jeans to abayas. Friends greet each other with هلا، شلونك؟; staff may say أهلاً وسهلاً or تفضل.

Basra Sports City is a broad complex of stadiums, paved approaches and open gathering space. Its dominant landmark, Basra International Stadium, has a rounded bowl and an exterior pattern of tall, branching supports reminiscent of palm trunks. Wide roads and pedestrian routes fill with cars and supporters on match days. Iraqi flags have horizontal red, white and black stripes, with green الله أكبر across the white stripe. In daylight, the stadium’s pale exterior casts distinct shadows; floodlights make the structure and pitch glow after dark. Crowd chants and clapping swell inside, while whistles and traffic are heard outside. Supporters greet friends with هلا and call to them يا أخوي.

Basra’s shanasheel are upper-storey wooden bays projecting over narrow streets, with closely spaced lattice screens, carved panels and small windows. Their timber may be dark brown, faded or painted, above older brick or plastered walls; neighbouring houses vary in condition rather than looking identically restored. The projecting rooms throw shade onto the walkway, and patterned sunlight passes through the screens into the rooms. In still, humid weather, fans and street voices are more audible than wind; old shutters may creak when opened. People pass below in everyday clothes or abayas. A neighbour might call السلام عليكم from a doorway and hear وعليكم السلام in reply.

Basra date palm farms have tall, rough trunks topped by spreading green fronds. Palms stand in irregular rows beside irrigation channels, with damp soil near the water and dry, dusty ground beyond it. In fruiting season, heavy bunches of dates hang below the fronds, changing from green to yellow, amber or brown according to variety and ripeness. Fronds scrape and rustle in wind; pumps, insects and distant road traffic add to the sound. Water flows gently through channels and darkens the earth along their edges. Summer light is fierce, with deep shade beneath the crowns. Farm workers in practical clothes greet visitors with السلام عليكم or هلا، شلونك؟

Al-Hadba rises beside Mosul’s Al-Nuri Mosque: a tall, tapering brick minaret with a slight, unmistakable lean and bands of raised geometric brickwork. Its reconstructed surface is warm beige, with diamond and zigzag patterns that sharpen in low afternoon light. The base is broad and square; the shaft narrows toward its cap. Around it are mosque walls, paved approaches and the closely built streets of Mosul’s old west bank. People pause to photograph it while others walk past shopfronts bearing Arabic signs. Footsteps and traffic mix with conversation and the call to prayer. A local greeting is “السلام عليكم,” answered “وعليكم السلام.”

Mosul University occupies a large campus on the city’s east bank, with broad internal roads, paved footpaths, lawns and mature trees between rectangular concrete and stone-faced academic buildings. Lecture blocks have repeated window rows and shaded entrances; Arabic faculty signs and campus noticeboards appear along busy walkways. Students carry backpacks, notebooks and phones, wearing everyday shirts, jeans, long dresses or headscarves. Groups gather in patches of shade, then stream through doors when classes begin. Shoes scrape on paving; conversations, car engines and classroom voices overlap. Bright summer sun casts hard building shadows, while winter brings softer, cooler light. Students commonly greet one another with “هلا” or “شلونك؟”

Ghabat is Mosul’s wooded recreation area near the Tigris, where planted trees make irregular bands of shade against the city’s dry, pale ground. Tall trunks, dusty paths, patches of grass and simple picnic spots frame views of family groups and parked cars. Leaves flutter in a light breeze, but loose soil rises in small puffs under shoes and tyres. People spread mats, pour tea and call to children playing nearby; casual clothes and colourful headscarves are common. Expect birds, voices, rustling leaves and distant traffic rather than deep-forest silence. Summer light is harsh beyond the trees. Friends may arrive saying “هلا بيكم” or “شلونكم؟”

Bab al-Saray is a dense market area in old Mosul, with narrow lanes, close-set shopfronts and Arabic signs above displays spilling toward pedestrians. Metal shutters, weathered masonry, fabric awnings and hanging goods compress the view; sunlight reaches the lane in bright strips. Stalls may show spices, clothing, household items or stacked produce, with their colours standing out against dusty beige walls. Shoppers move slowly around one another while porters carry parcels through the gaps. Bargaining, footsteps, shopkeepers’ calls and the rattle of shutters form a continuous sound. Men and women wear ordinary city clothes, including headscarves. A shopkeeper might say “تفضل” to invite someone in.

Villages across the Nineveh Plains sit amid open wheat fields and dry farmland east and northeast of Mosul. Low houses of pale stone, plaster or concrete block cluster beside narrow roads; water tanks, boundary walls, church bell towers and mosque minarets vary from settlement to settlement. Arabic, Syriac and Kurdish lettering may appear on signs, reflecting the area’s different communities. Tractors and small cars kick up dust, while wind ripples crops and carries birdsong across the flat ground. People wear everyday rural and town clothing, from work trousers to long dresses and headscarves. Greetings include Arabic “السلام عليكم,” Syriac “ܫܠܡܐ” (shlama) and Kurdish “سلاو” (slaw).

The monastery above Alqosh, commonly called Rabban Hormizd Monastery, clings to a steep, pale limestone mountainside. Its stone walls, small arched openings, stepped paths and chambers cut into rock look compact against the much larger cliff. From below, the buildings appear stacked along ledges rather than laid out on a level courtyard. Dry slopes and scattered scrub surround them; strong sun turns the rock nearly white and throws deep shadows into recesses. Visitors climb carefully, their steps scraping on stone, while wind and distant voices carry across the slope. The site belongs to the area’s Christian heritage. A local greeting may be Syriac “ܫܠܡܐ” (shlama) or Arabic “أهلاً وسهلاً.”

Bashiqa is a town northeast of Mosul, with low concrete and stone buildings, shop signs in Arabic and roads edged by olive groves. Small shops, passing cars and people buying bread give its centre a steady daytime bustle; outside town, dusty ground and rows of silvery-green olive leaves dominate. Yazidi shrines in the area have distinctive narrow, fluted conical spires, alongside the buildings of other local communities. An Iraqi flag, where flown, has horizontal red, white and black stripes with green “الله أكبر” centred on the white. Summer light is bright and dry; engines, conversation and leaves in the wind are typical sounds. Greetings include “السلام عليكم” and “شلونك؟”

Sinjar Mountain forms a long, rugged ridge above the flatter plains of western Nineveh. Its exposed rock looks beige, grey and reddish-brown, cut by gullies and sparse scrub; small settlements and cultivated patches lie along the lower slopes. From a distance the ridge has a broad, uneven silhouette rather than a single pointed summit. Roads bend around the terrain, and passing vehicles raise dust that drifts before settling. People in nearby communities wear practical everyday clothes and may speak Arabic or Kurdish Kurmanji. Wind is prominent on open slopes, with occasional goats, birds and distant engines audible. Summer sun is stark; winter can bring cold air and occasional snow. A Kurmanji greeting is “roj baş.”

Erbil Citadel rises on a broad, steep-sided mound above the flat city centre. At night, amber floodlights wash its long ochre-brick outer facades, making the small windows and stepped roofline stand out against a dark blue sky. The entrance ramp climbs toward a large arched gateway; below it, people cross the open plaza or pause for photographs. Kurdish and Arabic shop signs glow around the surrounding streets. Car tyres hiss on pavement, with voices and occasional horns below the quieter ramp. Visitors wear casual clothes, and some women wear colourful Kurdish dresses. A greeting might be “سڵاو، چۆنی؟” (hello, how are you?).

Beside Erbil Citadel, Qaysari bazaar is a dense network of narrow covered passages. Low arches and closely packed shopfronts frame displays of folded fabrics, Kurdish clothing, spices, sweets, jewellery and household goods. Fluorescent tubes and warm shop lamps illuminate the merchandise while the roof keeps direct sun off the walkways. Arabic and Kurdish lettering appears above counters and on hanging signs. Shoppers slow to squeeze past one another; fabric sways when lifted, and plastic bags rustle over the sound of bargaining and footsteps. A shopkeeper may say “سڵاو، بەخێربێیت” (hello, welcome), addressing a customer as “کاک” or “خانم”.

Ankawa, in northern Erbil, has broad paved streets lined with low-rise homes, apartment blocks, cafés, restaurants and brightly lit shopfronts. Churches, including St Joseph Cathedral, give parts of the neighbourhood a distinct silhouette of crosses and pale stone or concrete facades. Signs may combine Arabic, Kurdish, Syriac and English. In the evening, cars move between parked vehicles while diners gather at pavement tables; headlights sweep across walls and glass. People wear contemporary everyday clothes, with some dressed up for dinner or church. Conversation, clinking cups and traffic overlap. Greetings include “سڵاو” in Kurdish and “السلام عليكم” in Arabic; “كاک” is a respectful form of address.

Erbil’s 100 Meter Road is a wide ring road with separated carriageways, multiple lanes, planted medians and large junctions. Shopping centres, car showrooms, offices and newer apartment towers sit back from stretches of asphalt and service roads. Roadside signs use Kurdish, Arabic and English; after dark, illuminated storefronts and rows of streetlights reflect on car roofs. Traffic flows quickly between signals, then bunches at exits, with a steady tyre hum, engines and intermittent horns. In summer, hard midday sun bleaches the concrete and throws short shadows. Drivers and passengers wear ordinary city clothes; at a roadside shop, “سڵاو” and “بەخێربێیت” are everyday greetings.

Shanidar Park is a green public space within Erbil’s built-up streets, with lawns, mature shade trees and paved walking paths. The Shanidar Gallery is a recognisable cultural building beside the park’s planted areas. In warm weather, families spread out on the grass while others stroll or sit in the shade; leaves shift lightly, but the surrounding buildings remain still in the heat. Daylight filters through branches in irregular patches, and evening lamps pick out the paths. Expect children’s voices, footsteps, nearby traffic and quiet conversation, not wilderness sounds. Visitors wear casual clothes, including Kurdish dress on some outings. Friends may greet each other with “سڵاو، چۆنی؟”.

Azadi Park in Sulaymaniyah has open lawns, clusters of trees and paved paths used by walkers and families. Benches and gathering spots sit within sight of the city’s surrounding buildings; beyond them, hills frame the horizon. On bright days, tree shadows cut across the paths, while evenings bring softer light and more people outdoors. Children run across the grass, adults stroll or stop to talk, and birdsong mixes with traffic from beyond the park. Clothing ranges from jeans and shirts to Kurdish dresses and traditional men’s outfits. In the local Sorani Kurdish, people greet one another with “سڵاو، چۆنی؟” and may address a man respectfully as “کاک”.

Chavi Land is an amusement park on the hillside above Sulaymaniyah. Its Ferris wheel, other rides and cable-car gondolas make strong silhouettes against the mountain slope, with the city spread below. Gondolas glide along taut cables; the wheel turns slowly while smaller rides accelerate, pause and reverse according to their mechanisms. After sunset, coloured lights trace ride frames and flash against the dark hillside. Families queue near ticket booths and snack stands, wearing everyday clothes or dressed for an evening outing. Music, excited voices, mechanical hums and bursts of laughter carry through the open air. A local greeting is “سڵاو، بەخێربێیت” (hello, welcome).

Duhok Dam Lake fills a valley beside the city, its blue-green water edged by pale, dry hills and sparse shrubs. The dam is a broad sloping earth-and-rock embankment rather than a thin concrete wall. Shorelines change with the water level, exposing bands of light-coloured ground; in still weather, the hills reflect softly, while wind breaks the surface into small ripples. Cars and visitors gather at accessible viewpoints, with conversation and distant traffic more noticeable than any sound from the water. Summer light is sharp and the slopes look dusty; cooler months bring greener patches. People dress casually. In local Kurmanji Kurdish, “Silav, tu çawa yî?” means “Hello, how are you?”

Kirkuk Citadel rises on a broad earthen mound above the surrounding streets. Its old lanes are narrow and uneven, with weathered brick, plastered walls, recessed doorways and occasional arches. Below it, the Qaysariya market has closely spaced shops beneath covered passages; textiles hang in vertical folds and metal trays catch strips of daylight. Arabic and Kurdish shop signs appear among the storefronts. Shoppers in shirts, long dresses, abayas and Kurdish dress move slowly around stacked goods while vendors call across the passage. Footsteps, conversation and the rattle of rolling shutters echo under the roof; outside, the light is brighter and dustier.

At Baba Gurgur near Kirkuk, natural gas burns at vents close to the ground rather than from a tall torch. Small yellow-orange flames flicker and lean with the wind above rough, pale earth and darkened, scorched patches; heat makes the air immediately behind them shimmer. The surrounding terrain is open and low, with sparse vegetation and an industrial oil-field context in the distance. In daylight the flames can look modest against the sky, while at dusk their colour and movement become clearer. A faint rushing or hissing accompanies the combustion, mixed with wind across the exposed ground. Visitors keep back from the hot vents.

The Imam Ali shrine stands amid Najaf’s dense streets, its gold-clad dome and two gold-clad minarets rising above gates, arcades and nearby roofs. Sunlight flashes on the gilding; inside, polished stone floors, patterned tile, Arabic calligraphy and mirrored decoration reflect a cooler, softer light. Visitors enter respectfully, many wearing black or modest light-coloured clothing; women commonly wear abayas and head coverings. Shoes are left at designated places before entering prayer areas. People walk, pause and pray without hurried movement. The sound is a layered murmur of greetings, footsteps and recitation, quieter within the interior than on the streets outside.

Najaf’s old market is a long, busy passage near the Imam Ali shrine, with compact shops opening directly onto the pedestrian route. A high covered roof filters the harsh sun into bands of light across worn paving. Displays include hanging black abayas, folded cloth, prayer beads, perfume bottles and trays of agate rings; gold-coloured Arabic shop lettering sits above glass cases and shutters. Pilgrims and local shoppers move in both directions, pausing abruptly at counters, while shopkeepers call prices and greetings in Arabic. Fabric brushes past shoulders in the narrower stretches. Voices, footsteps, small purchases and rolling shutters form a constant enclosed-market sound.

Kufa Mosque is a broad, low complex with a large open courtyard, long arcaded edges and minarets visible above the outer walls. Pale stone paving reflects strong daylight; shaded arches, brickwork, decorative tile and Arabic inscriptions give the perimeter a cooler, more detailed texture. The associated shrine of Muslim ibn Aqil is within the complex. Worshippers cross the courtyard at an unhurried pace, then stop at designated prayer places; many wear modest Iraqi clothing, and women commonly wear abayas and head coverings. In the open air, footsteps and quiet recitation mix with wind, while voices gain a soft echo beneath the arcades.

The Imam Hussein shrine in Karbala is recognisable by its gilded dome and minarets above an extensive complex of gates and arcades. Gold surfaces glow warmly in direct sun and shine against the night sky under floodlights. Courtyards have smooth stone paving, decorative tile and Arabic calligraphy; interior surfaces include polished stone and intricate reflective ornament. Pilgrims in modest dress move steadily through the entrances, often in family groups; many women wear black abayas. Some stop to pray or read quietly, leaving passage clear for others. Footsteps, soft conversation and recitation blend into a continuous murmur, with more echo beneath covered sections.

Bayn al-Haramayn is the broad pedestrian space linking the Imam Hussein and al-Abbas shrines in Karbala. From the walkway, gilded domes and minarets mark the two ends, framed by shrine gates, arcades and Arabic signs. Pale paving spreads across a mostly level route that fills with moving pilgrims, families and attendants; people pause at the sides while others continue through the centre. Black abayas are common, alongside other modest clothing. Daylight reflects strongly off the stone, while evening lighting gives the domes a warm glow. The sound is open and layered: thousands of footsteps, low conversation, recitation and occasional calls carrying across the space.

Hillah’s old market is a network of close-set shopfronts and covered passages in the older commercial centre. Weathered brick and plaster sit behind metal shutters, Arabic signs, fabric awnings and roof panels that break the midday sun into uneven patches. Produce crates, household goods, hanging garments and small counters narrow the walking space. Shoppers in everyday Iraqi dress step around one another and stop to inspect goods; vendors lift boxes, rearrange displays and call to customers in Arabic. The air is warm and often dusty near the street openings. Footsteps, bargaining voices, passing handcarts and the clink of shop fittings overlap beneath the covers.

At Babylon near Hillah, show the reconstructed gate as a tall, rectangular entrance with deep-blue brickwork, a central passage and patterned rows of raised bulls and long-necked dragons. Brick joints and uneven colour keep the surface from looking like smooth plastic. Sandy reconstructed walls and dusty paths frame it; do not portray it as the original gate displayed in Berlin. Visitors in everyday shirts, abayas or dishdashas pause for photographs. Footsteps scuff gravel, voices carry softly and dry wind moves through the opening. In bright Iraqi sun, the blue stands sharply against beige earth.

Kish, near Babylon, reads as a spread of low archaeological mounds rather than a standing city. At Tell al-Uhaymir, reddish-brown brick remains rise above pale, dusty ground; elsewhere, eroded mudbrick edges, shallow trenches and scattered pottery fragments interrupt the flat plain. Keep the horizon wide, with sparse scrub and no invented intact palace. Sunlight makes the clay look warm orange by late afternoon, while wind lifts fine dust around shoes. Small groups of visitors or site workers move carefully over uneven ground. Their footsteps crunch on grit; nearby conversation is more audible than the quiet ruins.

Nippur, called Nuffar locally, appears as broad, weathered mounds on the flat plain of Al-Qadisiyyah. The former temple area is a broken mass of tan mudbrick, not a complete stepped ziggurat. Low ridges, exposed brick courses and excavation cuts cast short shadows in hard midday light. Dry soil powders underfoot; a breeze rasps through sparse plants and carries distant road or farm sounds. Visitors wear ordinary Iraqi clothes, with hats or scarves for the sun, and walk around fragile edges rather than across them. A greeting may be السلام عليكم, answered وعليكم السلام. No ancient city flag exists here.

Uruk, or Warka, is a vast field of low mudbrick mounds and excavation areas in southern Iraq, not a preserved street grid of tall buildings. Show broad, dusty expanses, broken wall lines, exposed rectangular bricks and the eroded rises of its temple precincts under an open sky. The colours run from pale beige to rusty brown; heat haze softens the distant horizon in summer. A few visitors or archaeologists provide scale, stepping cautiously on firm paths as grit shifts beneath their shoes. Wind and quiet Arabic conversation dominate the sound. Locals may greet one another with السلام عليكم or هلا.

Taq Kasra near Salman Pak is an enormous standing brick arch with a deep, high barrel vault. Its curved opening dwarfs people; narrow horizontal brick courses, missing sections and rough, jagged surviving walls prevent it from looking newly built. Warm brown masonry catches low sun, while the inside of the vault falls into broad shade. Show open ground around the monument rather than a complete ancient palace. Visitors in everyday Iraqi clothes stand back to photograph its scale. Their voices echo faintly beneath the arch; shoes scrape dust and wind moves across the site. A casual greeting is السلام عليكم.

Hatra southwest of Mosul is a broad stone archaeological site rising from a dry, open landscape. Its surviving temple complex has thick pale-beige masonry, tall vaulted openings, carved architectural details and broken wall tops; surrounding ruins are much lower. Avoid filling every gap with intact roofs. Bright sun cuts dark shapes inside the deep arches, and weathered blocks show irregular edges rather than polished faces. A few visitors or site staff walk slowly through courtyards, their steps tapping on stone and crunching on grit. Wind crosses the open ground; Arabic voices sound briefly hollow near an entrance. People may say السلام عليكم when meeting.

Nimrud, south of Mosul, is an archaeological mound with exposed mudbrick, stone foundations and damaged monumental remains, not an intact Assyrian palace. Show broken masonry, low wall lines, scattered carved fragments and protected work areas where appropriate. Any winged-bull sculpture must match a particular surviving or restored piece; do not populate every doorway with pristine statues. The surrounding plain is dusty, with sparse vegetation and a wide, bright sky. Site workers or visitors move cautiously among uneven stones. Gravel crunches beneath shoes, wind brushes loose soil and people speaking Arabic may greet each other with السلام عليكم.

Assur, at Qal'at Sherqat, sits above the Tigris on a high, weathered archaeological mound. Show eroded tan mudbrick walls, low excavated foundations and rough brick masses against the river’s greenish water and sloping banks. The site is not a complete walled ancient capital: broad gaps and bare earth dominate. Strong sun gives brick faces sharp texture, while the river reflects moving points of light. Sparse scrub bends in the breeze; shoes scrape grit, and wind and distant water accompany quiet conversation. Visitors in contemporary Iraqi clothing keep to accessible routes. In Arabic, one greeting is السلام عليكم, answered وعليكم السلام.

The Al-Askari shrine rises above Samarra’s low beige buildings with a broad gold-clad dome, two gold minarets, tiled arches and Arabic calligraphy. Its polished courtyard reflects hard midday light; footsteps soften inside, where visitors speak quietly and recitation may be heard. Men commonly wear shirts or dishdashas, and many women wear black abayas and headscarves. Visitors greet one another with «السلام عليكم» and reply «وعليكم السلام». Nearby shop signs are Arabic. Any Iraqi flag shown has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on the white band.

topic: Tikrit Saddam-era palaces on the river
body: Along the Tigris in Tikrit, the former presidential palace complex comprises large cream-colored concrete buildings, broad terraces, repetitive arches and formal stairways above the riverbank. Show its present condition rather than an intact luxury resort: some structures have broken windows, damaged facades or empty interiors. River water moves slowly past muddy banks and palms; wind carries dust across open paved areas. People nearby wear everyday shirts, trousers, dishdashas or headscarves and may say «هلا» or «السلام عليكم». Arabic signs identify local roads. An Iraqi flag, if shown, has horizontal red, white and black bands and green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

Around Baqubah, orange trees stand in irrigated rows behind low walls and earthen paths. Their dark, glossy leaves cast dense shade; ripe fruit appears as scattered bright orange spheres, not a solid orange canopy. Narrow channels carry brownish water that glints in the sun, while palms and other fruit trees may share a garden. Leaves rustle, irrigation water trickles and traffic hums beyond the orchards. Workers may wear practical shirts, trousers and headscarves, greeting one another with «شلونك؟» and «هلا». Roadside signs use Arabic. An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

Kut Barrage stretches across the Tigris as a long, low concrete structure with repeated gate openings and a roadway above. Water presses against the upstream side, then churns and whitens below open gates; the sound is a steady rush rather than a waterfall’s deep roar. Metal railings, utilitarian control structures and Arabic road signs frame the crossing. On the banks, people in shirts, dishdashas, abayas and headscarves watch traffic or fish, exchanging «السلام عليكم» and «وعليكم السلام». Summer light is harsh, with dusty haze over the river. An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

At the marshland approaches east of Amarah, shallow channels break into reed beds and open patches of water. Tall green reeds bend in the wind; their dry lower stalks are tan. A narrow wooden boat can glide low in the water, leaving a V-shaped wake, while waterbirds call above the soft slap of water against its sides. Water extent changes with season and supply, so do not make every horizon flooded. Local people wear practical clothes, dishdashas or headscarves and say «هلا بيك» and «السلام عليكم». Arabic signs appear nearer town. An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

The road from Nasiriyah toward Ur runs through flat, dry ground, with low embankments, sparse scrub, utility poles and Arabic direction signs reading «أور» or «الناصرية». Cars and minibuses raise light dust when they leave the asphalt. Near the archaeological site, Ur’s stepped mud-brick ziggurat comes into view as a solid, angular mass, not a sharp pyramid. Midday sunlight washes the landscape pale; tires hum and wind brushes across the roadside. Travelers wear ordinary shirts, trousers, abayas or headscarves and greet others with «السلام عليكم». An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

In cultivated parts of Diwaniyah governorate, irrigated rice plots form shallow, level rectangles divided by low earthen bunds. Young plants stand as thin green blades above muddy water; later, heavier grain heads bow and turn straw-gold. Water moves through small channels, and a breeze ripples the plants in bands rather than shaking whole trees. The scene is seasonal: a harvested field is short stubble, not a year-round green paddy. Farmers in loose work clothes and headscarves may say «هلا» or «شلونك؟» over the sound of pumps and insects. An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

Beyond Samawah’s built-up streets, the desert edge opens into pale gravel, compacted earth and sparse low shrubs, with little shade and a wide, hazy horizon. Near town, concrete-block houses, roadside shops and Arabic signs give way to utility poles and open ground; do not replace this with towering dunes. The nearby Euphrates corridor is greener, with palms and cultivated patches. Wind skims loose dust across the road, while passing tires make a dry hiss. People wear light shirts, dishdashas, abayas or headscarves and greet visitors with «هلا بيك» or «السلام عليكم». An Iraqi flag has horizontal red, white and black bands, with green «الله أكبر» centered on white.

The Euphrates at Ramadi is a broad, slow-moving band of greenish-brown water, edged in places by concrete embankments and in others by reeds, palms, and exposed muddy soil. Along the corniche, people walk beside low railings while families sit near the water; small boats leave spreading V-shaped wakes. Across the river are low concrete buildings and palms rather than a continuous high-rise skyline. The light is harsh and pale at midday, warmer and longer-shadowed near sunset. Water laps softly against steps, with traffic and conversation behind it. Where displayed, Iraq’s flag has horizontal red, white, and black bands, with green الله أكبر across the white band.

Fallujah’s bridge crosses the Euphrates on a low, practical concrete roadway, with repeated supports descending into the water and simple roadside barriers. From the bank, its long horizontal line sits above greenish water, reeds, and patches of exposed earth; low buildings and palms appear beyond. Vehicles roll across in a steady stream, their tyre noise mixing with wind and water beneath the spans. Sunlight makes the concrete look almost white, while dust softens distant edges. Nearby signs use Arabic, including الفلوجة. If an Iraqi flag is visible, it has red, white, and black horizontal bands and green الله أكبر on the white band.

Lake Qadisiyah spreads upstream of Haditha Dam as a wide blue-green reservoir between dry, pale limestone and gravel slopes. Its irregular shore forms coves and shallow inlets; wind makes tight ripples that flash silver in strong sun. The dam itself is a vast earth-and-rock embankment, with engineered concrete sections and service roads, not a thin wall between cliffs. Sparse shrubs dot the surrounding western Iraqi landscape, and the open sky takes up much of the view. At the water’s edge, waves make a light slapping sound; nearer the dam, vehicles and machinery add a low hum. Any displayed Iraqi flag is red, white, and black in horizontal bands, with green الله أكبر across the white band.

Near Heet, natural bitumen seeps emerge from rough, light-coloured ground as dark, glossy patches and small pools. The material looks nearly black, clings to stone, and moves slowly: bubbles swell, break, and leave rounded, sticky-looking surfaces rather than splashing like water. Mineral staining marks the edges. The surrounding Euphrates district includes dusty paths, low earth-toned buildings, and date palms closer to cultivated ground. In hard afternoon light the bitumen reflects bright, sharp highlights against matte dust. Small bubbles make faint pops; wind and distant traffic are usually more audible. Nearby Arabic signage may spell the town هيت or هِيت.

Rutba is a low western Iraqi town set in an open, stony desert. Flat-roofed concrete buildings, beige boundary walls, small shops, and fuel stops line broad, dusty roads used by cars and long-distance trucks. Arabic shop signs sit above metal shutters; beyond the built-up streets, the horizon is mostly level rock and sand with sparse scrub, not dunes. Strong sun casts short, crisp shadows, while wind lifts grit along kerbs and truck tyres hiss on asphalt. People wear everyday shirts and trousers, with some men in dishdashas. Greetings include السلام عليكم and the Iraqi شلونك؟ Iraq’s flag, when displayed, is red, white, and black in horizontal bands, with green الله أكبر across the white band.

Al-Qaim lies by the Euphrates near Iraq’s border with Syria. Its streets have low concrete houses, shopfronts with Arabic lettering, boundary walls, utility poles, and passing cars and trucks. Along the river, palms and cultivated plots bring green into an otherwise dry, sandy landscape. Midday light washes pale walls bright; evenings give the river a copper reflection. Expect tyre noise, shop conversations, and wind through palm fronds. People wear ordinary shirts and trousers or dishdashas, and greet one another with السلام عليكم or شلونك؟ The Iraqi flag displayed locally has red, white, and black horizontal bands, with green الله أكبر across the white band.

Trebil is the Iraq–Jordan road crossing amid a wide, bare desert plateau. Long freight trucks queue on asphalt lanes beside low inspection buildings, concrete barriers, overhead signs, and broad shade canopies. Dust gathers at road edges; engines idle, air brakes hiss, and papers rustle at service windows. Signs on the Iraqi side use Arabic, often alongside English. Staff and drivers wear practical everyday clothing, and a greeting may be السلام عليكم. The Iraqi flag has red, white, and black horizontal bands with green الله أكبر across the white band. Across the border, Jordan’s flag has black, white, and green horizontal bands and a red hoist triangle containing a white seven-pointed star.

Safwan is the Iraqi crossing toward Kuwait, set on a flat, dusty southern plain. Highway lanes widen into truck queues and inspection areas with low offices, metal canopies, concrete dividers, and Arabic direction signs. Heat shimmer blurs distant vehicles; engines idle, horns sound briefly, and tyres crunch over grit at the road edge. Drivers and staff wear everyday work clothes or dishdashas and may greet each other with السلام عليكم or شلونك؟ Iraq’s flag has red, white, and black horizontal bands with green الله أكبر across the white band. Kuwait’s flag has green, white, and red horizontal bands joined to a black trapezoid at the hoist.

Beside an Iraqi highway, a kahwa is often a low concrete building with a corrugated-metal awning, plastic chairs, and a few parked cars or trucks on dusty ground. An Arabic sign may read استراحة or شاي وقهوة. Inside, small glasses of dark tea sit on metal saucers near a steaming samovar; a refrigerator hums behind a counter stocked with bottled water. Trucks pass with a low rush, stirring grit at the awning’s edge. In summer, harsh sun bleaches the forecourt while shade falls sharply beneath the roof. A server calls تفضل, and travellers answer with هلا or يعطيك العافية.

An Iraqi petrol station has a broad canopy over pump islands, a concrete forecourt darkened by tyre marks, and signs reading محطة وقود or بنزين. Pumps have digital displays, thick black hoses, and metal nozzles; a small kiosk may sell water and snacks. Cars queue nose to tail, and a worker guides each driver forward with an open hand before placing the nozzle in the tank. Engines idle, pumps click, and traffic sounds carry in from the road. In bright afternoon light, the canopy casts a hard rectangular shadow. Drivers commonly say السلام عليكم or عمي، فل, asking for a full tank.

An everyday Iraqi checkpoint narrows a road with concrete barriers, orange cones, and a small shaded booth. A sign in Arabic tells drivers to slow down; a uniformed officer stands beside the lane while another sits under the canopy. Cars roll forward one at a time, brake gently, then continue after a brief exchange or document check. Engines idle and tyres crunch over dusty pavement beneath the officer’s quiet directions. Sunlight catches the pale barriers, leaving the booth interior dim. A driver lowers the window and says السلام عليكم; the officer may reply وعليكم السلام، الهويات رجاءً. The mood is orderly and unhurried.

In a southern Iraqi village, a mudhif may be a long hall built from bundled reeds, with tall curved reed arches meeting overhead. Tightly woven mats cover the sides and floor, their tan fibres glowing gold where daylight enters through the doorway. Guests sit along the walls on rugs and cushions, leaving the centre open. A host pours bitter Arabic coffee from a long-spouted dallah into tiny finjan cups; cups tap softly and reeds rustle in a breeze. Outside are palms, packed earth, and sometimes marsh water nearby. A guest is welcomed with هلا بالضيف or تفضل, then offered a seat.

topic: Iraqi rooftop at night in summer
body: On a summer night, an Iraqi house roof is a flat concrete space edged by a low parapet. A plastic water tank, satellite dish, clothesline, and air-conditioning units break up its outline. Families may bring up thin mattresses, pillows, and a tray of tea to catch a breeze after the day’s heat. Fabric lifts gently on the line; a fan whirs where electricity is available. Neighbouring roofs sit close together beneath a hazy sky, with distant traffic and generator hum below. Warm streetlights pick out beige walls while windows glow across the lane. Someone calls تعالوا فوك, inviting the family upstairs.

An Iraqi home kitchen often has tiled walls, a metal cooker, stacked stainless-steel pots, and a steel gas cylinder standing upright beside the stove or just outside the kitchen door. The cylinder is commonly red or orange, with a scuffed painted surface, a top handle ring, and a regulator connected to a flexible hose. A pot of rice steams over a steady blue flame; its lid rattles softly when the water boils. Daylight from a small window catches the tile glaze, while a vent fan hums overhead. A cook moves a hot pot with a folded cloth and calls تفضلوا, inviting everyone to eat.

An Iraqi wedding street procession often forms a slow line of decorated cars moving through a neighbourhood. White ribbons or flowers may frame the lead car, while passengers wave through open windows. Horns sound in short, overlapping bursts; recorded wedding music and handclaps carry between concrete shopfronts and apartment balconies. Relatives in suits, dresses, and other festive clothes gather at the roadside, their faces lit by car headlights and phone screens after dark. The cars advance, pause, and advance again with traffic rather than moving in a perfect formation. Onlookers call مبروك and الله يتمم عليكم, and the couple’s family answers الله يبارك بيكم.

An Iraqi condolence tent is commonly a large fabric canopy set beside a home or in an open lot, with rows of plastic chairs over rugs or bare ground. Fabric panels block the sun, leaving soft, even shade; fans may stir the warm air. Guests arrive quietly, greet the family, sit, and accept small glasses of tea or water. Low conversation, footsteps, and sometimes a measured Qur’an recitation fill the space. Clothing is generally subdued, though styles vary by family and community. A visitor says عظّم الله أجركم or البقية بحياتكم; the family may reply أجرنا وأجركم or الله يسلمك.
